steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for an audio signal processing paper on scaling up learned adaptive filter optimizers, presenting our new meta-learning based adaptive filter method. Cover background on adaptive filters, scaling and neural approaches, our method and evaluation, and our contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. Adaptive filters and hand-designed optimizers
2. Scaling in deep learning; neural approaches to online adaptive filters
3. Our method and how we evaluate it
4. Contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. Adaptive filters (AF)
   - indispensable in signal processing: acoustic echo cancellation, equalization, interference suppression
   - time-varying filter weights; need update/optimization rule over time
   - improving AF performance = intricate challenge; nuanced optimizer design
   - designers rely on mathematical insight: from least mean squares (LMS) to the Kalman filter
2. Scaling
   - deep learning advances in other domains via "scaling"
   - scaling = improve existing method by deploying more compute
   - enticing: growing compute of modern smart devices, less manual tuning/intervention
   - neural nets for online low-latency AFs, two approaches:
     - model-based: DNNs in existing AF frameworks -> optimizer statistics, step-size, other quantities
     - model-free: no existing AF strategy; meta-learned optimizers end-to-end; state-of-the-art (SOTA) results
   - focus on model-free; but scaling limited to high-latency regimes or only marginal gains
3. Our method
   - new online AF method: supervised multi-step AF (SMS-AF)
   - series of algorithm improvements on top of recent meta-learning methods
   - scale performance via model capacity and/or inference cost (Fig. 1)
   - tasks: acoustic echo cancellation (AEC), generalized sidelobe canceller (GSC) speech enhancement; compare with recent SOTA
   - scaling -> substantial gains in all metrics across tasks and datasets; breakthrough AEC performance
4. Contributions
   - general purpose AF method; more computation -> reliably better performance
   - design insights for customizing to AEC and GSC
   - empirical exploration of AF optimizer scaling: model size, optimizer step count
   - insights on how approach generalizes Kalman filtering

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Adaptive filters (AF) have an indispensable role in a lot of signal processing applications, like acoustic echo cancellation, equalization, and interference suppression. AFs have time-varying filter weights as parameters, and they need an update or optimization rule to control the weights over time. It is still an intricate challenge to improve the performance of AFs, and it needs a nuanced approach to designing the optimizer. Because of this, AF algorithm designers have used mathematical insights to create tailored optimizers, starting with the least mean squares algorithm (LMS), which was foundational, and going up to the Kalman filter.

On the other hand, in other domains there have been countless remarkable advances in deep learning algorithms through the principle of “scaling”. In the scaling approach, an existing method is improved by using more computational resources. Scaling methods are attractive because they use the growing computational capabilities of modern smart devices, and they reduce the need for manual tuning and intervention, which is labor-intensive. For neural networks for online low-latency AFs that can benefit from scaling, there are two general approaches. 1) model-based methods, which put deep neural networks (DNNs) into existing AF frameworks to update optimizer statistics, step-size, or other quantities. 2) model-free strategies, which do not rely on an existing AF strategy and learn AF optimizers end-to-end with meta-learning, and which give state-of-the-art (SOTA) results. We focus on the second kind because they have been successful recently, but scaling these approaches has either been limited to high-latency regimes or only improves results a little.

[our method]
- new online AF method: supervised multi-step AF (SMS-AF)
- algorithm improvements on top of recent meta-learning methods -> scale performance by model capacity and/or inference cost (Fig. 1)
- evaluate on acoustic echo cancellation (AEC) + generalized sidelobe canceller (GSC) speech enhancement vs recent SOTA
- substantial gains in all metrics across tasks/datasets; breakthrough AEC performance

[contributions]
- general purpose AF method: more computation -> reliably better
- design insights for AEC and GSC
- empirical scaling exploration: model size, optimizer step count
- insights on generalizing Kalman filtering

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Adaptive filters (AF) have an indispensable role in a lot of signal processing applications, like acoustic echo cancellation, equalization, and interference suppression. AFs have time-varying filter weights as parameters, and they need an update or optimization rule to control the weights over time. It is still an intricate challenge to improve the performance of AFs, and it needs a nuanced approach to designing the optimizer. Because of this, AF algorithm designers have used mathematical insights to create tailored optimizers, starting with the least mean squares algorithm (LMS), which was foundational, and going up to the Kalman filter.

On the other hand, in other domains there have been countless remarkable advances in deep learning algorithms through the principle of “scaling”. In the scaling approach, an existing method is improved by using more computational resources. Scaling methods are attractive because they use the growing computational capabilities of modern smart devices, and they reduce the need for manual tuning and intervention, which is labor-intensive. For neural networks for online low-latency AFs that can benefit from scaling, there are two general approaches. 1) model-based methods, which put deep neural networks (DNNs) into existing AF frameworks to update optimizer statistics, step-size, or other quantities. 2) model-free strategies, which do not rely on an existing AF strategy and learn AF optimizers end-to-end with meta-learning, and which give state-of-the-art (SOTA) results. We focus on the second kind because they have been successful recently, but scaling these approaches has either been limited to high-latency regimes or only improves results a little.

We propose a new online AF method that we call supervised multi-step AF (SMS-AF). Our method adds a series of algorithm improvements on top of recent meta-learning methods, and together they make it possible to scale performance by increasing model capacity and/or inference cost, as shown in Fig. 1. We evaluate the approach on acoustic echo cancellation (AEC) and on generalized sidelobe canceller (GSC) speech enhancement and compare it to recent SOTA approaches. The results show that the scaling behavior gives substantial performance gains in all metrics across tasks and datasets and that it delivers breakthrough AEC performance.

Our contributions are: 1) A new general purpose AF method where we can reliably improve performance just by using more computation, 2) Design insights for customizing the proposed method for AEC and GSC, 3) Empirical exploration of AF optimizer scaling that shows our approach scales with model size and with optimizer step count, and 4) Insights on how our approach generalizes Kalman filtering.

Adaptive filters (AF) have an indispensable role in a lot of signal processing applications, like acoustic echo cancellation, equalization, and interference suppression. AFs have time-varying filter weights as parameters, and they need an update or optimization rule to control the weights over time. It is still an intricate challenge to improve the performance of AFs, and it needs a nuanced approach to designing the optimizer. Because of this, AF algorithm designers have used mathematical insights to create tailored optimizers, starting with the least mean squares algorithm (LMS) [1], which was foundational, and going up to the Kalman filter [2,3,4,5].

On the other hand, in other domains there have been countless remarkable advances in deep learning algorithms through the principle of “scaling” [6,7,8,9]. In the scaling approach, an existing method is improved by using more computational resources. Scaling methods are attractive because they use the growing computational capabilities of modern smart devices, and they reduce the need for manual tuning and intervention, which is labor-intensive. For neural networks for online low-latency AFs that can benefit from scaling, there are two general approaches. 1) model-based methods, which put deep neural networks (DNNs) into existing AF frameworks to update optimizer statistics [10,11,12], step-size [13,14], or other quantities [15]. 2) model-free strategies, which do not rely on an existing AF strategy and learn AF optimizers end-to-end with meta-learning [16,17,18,19], and which give state-of-the-art (SOTA) results [15,19]. We focus on the second kind because they have been successful recently, but scaling these approaches has either been limited to high-latency regimes [18] or only improves results a little [15].

We propose a new online AF method that we call supervised multi-step AF (SMS-AF). Our method adds a series of algorithm improvements on top of recent meta-learning methods [17,18], and together they make it possible to scale performance by increasing model capacity and/or inference cost, as shown in Fig. 1. We evaluate the approach on acoustic echo cancellation (AEC) and on generalized sidelobe canceller (GSC) speech enhancement and compare it to recent SOTA approaches. The results show that the scaling behavior gives substantial performance gains in all metrics across tasks and datasets and that it delivers breakthrough AEC performance.

Our contributions are: 1) A new general purpose AF method where we can reliably improve performance just by using more computation, 2) Design insights for customizing the proposed method for AEC and GSC, 3) Empirical exploration of AF optimizer scaling that shows our approach scales with model size and with optimizer step count, and 4) Insights on how our approach generalizes Kalman filtering.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Adaptive filters (AF) play an indispensable role in a wide array of signal processing applications such as acoustic echo cancellation, equalization, and interference suppression. AFs are parameterized by time-varying filter weights and require an update or optimization rule to control them over time. Improving the performance of AFs remains an intricate challenge that requires a nuanced approach to optimizer design. Consequently, AF algorithm designers have relied on mathematical insights to create tailored optimizers, from the foundational least mean squares algorithm (LMS) [1] to the Kalman filter [2,3,4,5].

In contrast, we have seen countless remarkable deep learning algorithm advancements in other domains through the principle of “scaling” [6,7,8,9]. The scaling approach improves an existing method by deploying additional computational resources. Scaling methods are particularly enticing, as they tap into the increasing computational capabilities of modern smart devices and minimize the need for labor-intensive manual tuning and intervention. For neural networks for online low-latency AFs that can benefit from scaling, we find two general approaches: 1) model-based methods that integrate deep neural networks (DNNs) into existing AF frameworks to update optimizer statistics [10,11,12], step-size [13,14], or other quantities [15] and 2) model-free strategies that do not rely on an existing AF strategy, learn AF optimizers end-to-end using meta-learning [16,17,18,19], and yield state-of-the-art (SOTA) results [15,19]. We focus on the latter, given their recent success, but note that scaling such approaches has either been limited to high-latency regimes [18] or only marginally improves results [15].

We propose a new online AF method called supervised multi-step AF (SMS-AF). Our method integrates a series of algorithm improvements on top of recent meta-learning methods [17,18] that together enable scaling performance by increasing model capacity and/or inference cost, as shown in Fig. 1. We evaluate our approach on acoustic echo cancellation (AEC) and generalized sidelobe canceller (GSC) speech enhancement and compare to recent SOTA approaches. Results show that our scaling behavior translates to substantial performance gains in all metrics across tasks and datasets and delivers breakthrough AEC performance.

Our contributions include: 1) A new general purpose AF method that allows us to reliably improve performance by simply using more computation, 2) Design insights for customizing our proposed method for AEC and GSC, 3) Empirical exploration of AF optimizer scaling showing that our approach scales with model size and optimizer step count, and 4) Insights into how our approach generalizes Kalman filtering.
